title: Strong opinions, weakly held: how to decide when to change a proven marketing message
summary: Jason Cohen reconciles two conflicting rules: always search for disproof of your beliefs, yet never change a proven strategy flippantly. His answer is that how weakly you hold an opinion should depend on how much work went into forming it. Illustrated with an AdWords specialist asking to change battle-tested landing page copy.

principles.text: Conviction is needed to act, but must be tempered by a constant search for disproof.
principles.quote: conviction, while necessary for action, must be tempered with a constant search for disproof.

principles.text: Being wishy-washy kills execution, but ignoring contrary evidence is irresponsible and dishonest.
principles.quote: Being wishy-washy is an impediment to inspiring people, working towards a goal, and getting things done, but turning a blind eye to contrary evidence is irresponsible and even dishonest.

principles.text: A strategy needs to be stable enough to execute but open enough to be corrected.
principles.quote: A strategy that changes all the time cannot be executed, but a strategy that never changes is definitely incorrect.

principles.text: Hold opinions more loosely when they were formed casually; change them readily if someone has a rationale.
principles.quote: some opinions were made without consideration. Why do we have a "Resources" web page separate from an "External Articles" page? No reason, it just ended up like that. So if someone else has a different idea and some rationale behind it, make the change.

principles.text: Opinions forged through testing, customer listening and debate deserve the same rigor to change as to create, and shouldn't be changed flippantly.
principles.quote: If it deserved this much consideration before, it deserves the same consideration now. Perhaps more.

principles.text: Don't use 'branding' as a shield against good ideas, but challenge new ideas against proven ones with proportionally high standards.
principles.quote: But when the existing ideas are proven, when great works have molded them, new ideas should be challenged with proportionally high standards.
